name: Tiananmen Square
label: Tiananmen Square
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/941596: large area 'Tian'anmen Square' (832 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: One of the largest public squares in the world.

text.description: Tiananmen Square is the huge open square in the middle of Beijing, named after the Tiananmen (Gate of Heavenly Peace) on its north side, which separates it from the Forbidden City. It photographs well because of its sheer scale and the big, formal buildings around it. The Monument to the People's Heroes, the Great Hall of the People, the National Museum of China and the Chairman Mao Memorial Hall all stand on or beside the square. Together with the Central Axis they were added to the UNESCO World Heritage list in 2024. The square was first laid out in 1651 and made about four times bigger in the 1950s. It now measures roughly 765 by 282 metres. A national flagpole stands at the northern end, and the flag is raised and lowered there every day at sunrise and sunset. For a phone, the challenge is that everything is wide and far apart. Pick one clear subject, such as the gate, the monument or the flag, and let the empty space around it show the size. Use the gridlines to keep the horizon and building edges straight. Expect people in most frames, so include a few as a sense of scale rather than waiting for a clear shot.
text.geographic_location: In the city centre of Beijing, directly south of the Tiananmen gate and the Forbidden City. The square is flanked by the Great Hall of the People to the west and the National Museum of China to the east.
text.directions_text: Tiananmen Square is in central Beijing, just south of the Tiananmen gate. No station is listed for this spot, so use a map app to reach the square. The phone icon on the map is about 1 minute on foot from the subject, a little to its west. The phone icon on the map is about 55 m west of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the width of the square, and use the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of a single building. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the gate, the flag or the monument from a distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 55 m west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face east. Stay on the open ground rather than close to the buildings so you can fit more in.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the horizon on the lower third, so the sky and the large buildings take up most of the frame. Pick one subject and leave empty space around it to show the scale. For a sweeping view of the whole square, try panorama mode, holding the phone level and turning slowly. Keep the telephoto for close shots of the flagpole or monument details.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the main building to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky looks washed out. In night mode, brace your elbows against your body and keep still for the few seconds it takes.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise and sunset are when the daily flag ceremonies happen, so they are good times for atmosphere, though the square can be busy then. Early or late in the day the light is also softer than at midday.

text.access_note: The square is a large public space, but entry arrangements and any restrictions can change, so check the official site before you go.

name: Forbidden City
label: Forbidden City
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '万春亭' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '万春亭' (way/685673149): middle (25 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/9511883: large area 'Forbidden City' (1322 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: The Ming and Qing imperial palace complex.

text.description: The Forbidden City was the imperial palace of the Ming and Qing emperors. It was built between 1406 and 1420 and was home to twenty-four emperors until 1924. It covers about 72 hectares, is now run as the Palace Museum, and has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1987. At ground level its size is hard to fit into a phone frame, so the best picture is taken from above. It marks the general area; the pavilion called 万春亭 on top of Jingshan Hill is nearby, and from there the whole palace spreads out below you to the south. You can follow the central axis through the rows of roofs, and the White Pagoda of Beihai is visible from the same spot. Guides call this the standard panorama of the palace, and it is the place most photographers aim for. Allow roughly 10 to 15 minutes to climb from the park's south entrance. Early morning or late afternoon suits it best. The pavilion is busiest around sunset and the front rail fills quickly, so arrive early if you want a clear spot. If you would like a street-level view instead, the palace's northwest and northeast corner towers rise above the moat and the red walls. On calm days the water gives a reflection of the northwest corner tower.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Beijing, inside the old Imperial City.
text.directions_text: Go to Jingshan Park, which lies just north of the Forbidden City. Enter by the park's south entrance and climb Jingshan Hill to the pavilion at the top. The climb takes roughly 10 to 15 minutes. From the pavilion, the palace lies straight ahead to the south. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the main view. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the full width of the palace will not fit, and to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out roofs and gates in the middle distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at 万春亭 (summit of Jingshan Hill, south side of the pavilion). The whole Forbidden City spread out below to the south, with the central axis and the White Pagoda of Beihai visible from the same spot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the central axis up with the middle of the frame. Keep a little sky at the top and the nearer roofs at the bottom so the palace looks as large as it is. Try one wide shot and one zoomed-in shot of the halls. For a sweep including the pagoda, use panorama mode and pan slowly. As an alternative, the northwest and northeast corner towers can be photographed from outside the palace, across the moat.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the palace to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky does not wash out. Hold the phone against the rail or your body to keep it steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon before sunset, or early morning. One guide says the hour before sunset gives the warmest light. The crowd peaks around sunset, so arrive early within that hour to get a place at the rail.

text.access_note: Jingshan Park charges an entrance fee, and entry to the Forbidden City itself is managed by the Palace Museum, so check the official sites for current prices and rules before you go.

name: Temple of Heaven
label: Temple of Heaven
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '丹陛桥' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '丹陛桥' (way/29182843): middle (366 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/24824550: large area 'Temple of Heaven' (2305 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.

text.description:
The Temple of Heaven is a large complex of imperial buildings in the southeastern part of central Beijing, where the Ming and Qing emperors came to pray for good harvests. It was first built in 1420 and its present layout was largely settled by 1749. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1998, and in 1918 it was opened to the public as a park. The grounds cover about 2.73 square kilometres, so it is worth choosing your pictures rather than trying to photograph everything.

The best-known building is the Hall of Prayer for Good Harvests: a round, triple-roofed hall 38 m tall, on three levels of marble, with dark blue roof tiles. It photographs well because everything is arranged along a single straight line. The Vermilion Steps Bridge (Danbi Bridge, 丹陛桥) is a raised walkway about 360 m long that rises slowly towards the Hall. Standing on it, you see a long, symmetrical path with the blue roof at the end.

For a second picture, try the Hall of Prayer from beside its red wall, which gives the classic Beijing palace look with fewer people in front. The Circular Mound Altar is a plain stone circle under open sky, and makes a simple, geometric contrast to the ornate halls. Keep your phone lens clean and give yourself time, as the park is big and the walking adds up.
text.geographic_location: The Temple of Heaven is in Dongcheng District, in the southeastern part of central Beijing, inside its own large walled park.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is given for this spot, so from central Beijing head towards the southeastern part of the city by taxi and ask for the Temple of Heaven (Tiantan, 天坛). Once you are inside the park, make your way to the Vermilion Steps Bridge (丹陛桥), the long raised walkway that runs between the Imperial Vault of Heaven and the Hall of Prayer. The Hall lies at its northern end. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the telephoto lens (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the main shot, because it squeezes the long bridge and the Hall together. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) only for a low, dramatic view of the stone path. The default lens (1x) is a good middle option if your phone has no telephoto.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on 丹陛桥 (middle of the bridge, facing north toward the Hall). The Hall of Prayer on the central axis at the end of a long, symmetrical path, with the bridge's stone leading the eye toward the blue roof. The recommended viewpoint inside the park is the middle of Danbi Bridge (丹陛桥), facing north towards the Hall.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: From the middle of the bridge, switch on gridlines and put the centre line of the path on the middle vertical line, so the Hall sits exactly in the centre. Keep the phone level so the symmetry looks right. Zoom in until the Hall fills the top third of the picture and the stone path fills the rest. For a different view, the Hall of Prayer from beside its red wall gives the classic palace look, and the Circular Mound Altar makes a simple stone-and-sky picture.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the blue roof to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out the roof tiles. Take a few shots in a row, because people walk across the bridge and you can choose the cleanest frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Check crowd levels on the day. The Hall can't be entered after about 6 pm, but it can be photographed from outside when lit; one guide says the park lights up on Friday and Saturday nights at 8 pm, so check before you rely on it. Use night mode and hold the phone steady against a railing or your body.

text.access_note: Entry to the park and its halls needs a ticket, and some areas may be closed or under works, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Telephoto lenses at 2x-5x are available on many but not all phones; the reader may need to use the default lens (1x) and crop.
Some guides say the park lights up on Friday and Saturday nights at 8 pm; check before you rely on it.

name: Tiananmen
label: Tiananmen Gate
camera_source: Commons cluster (23 photos). Moved 24 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 440 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/8847697: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Gate of Heavenly Peace' (126 m across).
notes: The Gate of Heavenly Peace with Mao's portrait, at the entrance to the Forbidden City.

text.description: Tiananmen, the Gate of Heavenly Peace, is the great red-walled gatehouse at the front of the Forbidden City and the old Imperial City. It is one of the most recognisable buildings in China. It photographs well because the shape is so clear: a wide red base with a double-roofed tower of yellow-glazed tiles on top, with stone bridges, carved lions and two white marble columns (huabiao) in front. The first gate on this spot dates from 1420 in the Ming dynasty. It burned down and was rebuilt more than once, and it took its present name in 1651. The building is about 66 m long, 37 m wide and 32 m high. In 1949 Mao Zedong proclaimed the People's Republic of China from its balcony, and a large portrait of him hangs above the central passage today. The gate sits on the north side of Tiananmen Square, with the broad Chang'an Avenue running between them. For a phone photo, the main challenge is distance and crowds. From the phone icon on the map you see the whole gate with the square around it, but at the default lens (1x) the gate looks small, so use the telephoto to bring it closer. Keep the phone level so the long horizontal roofline does not slope. The moat and its fountains in front of the gate can add a pleasant foreground if you step closer.
text.geographic_location: Tiananmen is in the centre of Beijing. It stands at the northern edge of Tiananmen Square, across Chang'an Avenue, and is the front entrance to the Forbidden City.
text.directions_text: No station is listed for this spot, so head for Tiananmen Square in the centre of Beijing. The phone icon on the map is about 440 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Telephoto (3x-5x if your phone has it, otherwise 2x). The default lens (1x) shows the gate as a small band in a wide square.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 440 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. From here you can fit the whole width of the gate and its double roof in one frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Zoom until the gate fills about half the width of the frame, and keep the central passage and the portrait in the middle. Turn on gridlines and line the roof edge up with a horizontal line so it stays level. Wait for a gap in the people crossing the square, or include a few of them to show the scale. For a wider scene with the square, take one shot at the default lens (1x) too.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the red wall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out the roof tiles. Hold the phone with both hands, as zoomed shots show every small shake.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows. Early in the day is often quieter. Avoid midday haze if you can.

text.access_note: The square and the gate are a major public site and may have security checks or restrictions, and going up into the gate may need a ticket, so check the official site before you go.

name: Beijing National Stadium
label: Bird's Nest
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '龙形水系' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/152301551: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'National Stadium' (449 m across).

text.description:
The Bird's Nest is the stadium built for the 2008 Summer Olympics, and it still looks unlike any other building in Beijing. A tangle of grey steel beams wraps around a red concrete seating bowl, so the outside looks like woven twigs. The design came from the Swiss architects Herzog & de Meuron, who studied Chinese ceramics while developing it. It opened on 28 June 2008, holds around 80,000 people, and was used again for the 2022 Winter Olympics.

The best photo for most visitors is the evening view from the lakeside on the north side of the dragon-shaped water system. At dusk the lit steel glows and is mirrored in the water, and the Water Cube and Olympic Tower often fit into the same frame. The phone icon on the map marks the middle of the stadium, so the lakeside on the north side of the water system is a recommended place to shoot from rather than the stadium itself. If you arrive earlier in the day, South Gate Square gives the classic front-on view of the facade in soft daylight. Datu Road Bridge gives a wider panorama with the rest of the Olympic Park around the stadium.

The stadium is huge, so give yourself room to step back and keep the whole outline in the frame. Look for the reflection near the water's edge, and wait a few minutes after the lights come on, when the sky still has some colour. The stadium is the star, so keep the water and the lamps at the edges of the picture.
text.geographic_location: The stadium stands at the Olympic Green in Chaoyang district, Beijing, in the Olympic Park beside the Water Cube and the Olympic Tower.
text.directions_text: Head for the Olympic Park and Olympic Green area in Chaoyang; check a map app for the best way to reach Olympic Park. From the park, walk to the lakeside on the north side of the dragon-shaped water system and face the stadium from there. The stadium is the large steel building you can see across the water, so it is hard to miss once you are in the park. Check the spot on a map before you set off, as the name of the water system may be written differently on signs. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close to the water and want the whole stadium and its reflection in one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural view, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the pattern of the steel or to isolate the Olympic Tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. For the recommended view, walk to the lakeside on the north side of the dragon-shaped water system and face the stadium across the water. From here the lit stadium is mirrored in the water, often with the Water Cube and Olympic Tower in the same frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the water's edge on a lower line so the stadium and its reflection fill the picture. Keep the camera level so the building does not lean. For a different view, try South Gate Square for a front-on daytime shot, or Datu Road Bridge for a wide panorama.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the steel to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the lights keep their detail and the sky stays dark blue. After dark, use night mode and rest your elbows on a railing or wall to keep the phone still. Try a Live Photo if people or ripples are moving in the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Around dusk, as the stadium lights come on. One guide suggests waiting by the water for the lights to switch on.

text.access_note: Viewing the outside from the public areas of Olympic Park is free, but the interior and rooftop Skywalk are ticketed and may close during events, so check the official site before you go.

name: Great Hall of the People
label: Great Hall of People
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Great Hall of the People' (1 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/8848388: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Great Hall of the People' (404 m across).
notes: Government building on the west side of Tiananmen Square.

text.description:
The Great Hall of the People is the big, pale, flat-roofed building on the west side of Tiananmen Square. It is where China's National People's Congress meets each March, and it is also used for ceremonies and large events. It opened in September 1959 as one of the "Ten Great Constructions" for the tenth anniversary of the People's Republic, and the building work took only ten months. It is huge: about 356 metres long and 206.5 metres wide, rising to 46.5 metres at its highest point. The national emblem hangs at the eaves above the main gate.

It photographs well because of its scale and its steady rhythm of tall columns and glazed eaves. The usual picture is the full frontal view, which is very busy. For something calmer, one travel guide suggests the steps outside the East Gate, which it describes as less crowded. If you can find that spot, you may get the facade and entrance at closer range, possibly with fewer people in the frame. Keep the lines of the columns straight and let the emblem and roof edge sit near the top of the picture. If you want the classic full-front shot as well, it is worth taking that once as a comparison. For a wide view of the hall together with the square and the National Museum, Tiananmen Square is the other spot to try.

Expect security staff and crowds. Be patient, take a few frames, and keep moving along the paved areas rather than stopping in walkways.
text.geographic_location: In central Beijing, on the west side of Tiananmen Square, facing the National Museum across the square.
text.directions_text: Head for the Tiananmen Square area and finish on foot, walking to the square's western edge, where the Great Hall of the People fills the whole side. One travel guide suggests the steps outside the East Gate as a vantage point, so look for that side of the building. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full facade and the row of columns, then switch to the default lens (1x) for the entrance. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the national emblem under the eaves.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. A travel guide suggests the steps outside the East Gate as a quieter angle, so look for that side of the building. From there the facade and entrance should sit right in front of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the columns with the vertical lines so the building does not lean. Keep the entrance in the centre and leave some sky above the roof. If you want the classic full-front view or a wide panorama of the square, you can also take those from Tiananmen Square as an alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the pale facade to set focus, then pull the exposure slider down slightly so the stonework keeps its detail and the sky is not washed out. Wipe the lens first, as crowds and dust can leave a haze.

text.access_note: You can photograph the outside without a ticket, but security checks are strict, and going inside needs advance booking, so check the official site before you go.

name: Yonghe Temple
label: Lama Temple
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '雍和门' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '雍和门' (way/177053582): middle (31 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/24825312: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Lama Temple' (450 m across).

text.description:
Yonghe Temple, also called the Lama Temple, is a working Tibetan Buddhist monastery in Dongcheng District, Beijing. Its buildings mix Han Chinese and Tibetan styles, and it is one of the largest monasteries of its kind in China proper. Building began in 1694 in the Qing dynasty. It started as a princely residence, and the future Yongzheng Emperor lived here before he took the throne. Later, under the Qianlong Emperor, the roofs were given yellow tiles, a colour reserved for the emperor, and in 1744 the palace was turned into a monastery. The main buildings run along a north–south line about 480 metres long, with a courtyard between each hall.

It photographs well because of the colour: red walls, golden roof tiles and carved timber, all set close together. The temple's entrance archway makes a natural frame, with the courtyard stretching away behind it. Once you are in the courtyards, look up for details on the eaves and roof ridges. Photography is not allowed inside the halls or of the Buddha statues in the Wanfu Pavilion, so plan on exterior pictures. For a quieter alternative, the old Imperial Academy street nearby has red walls and green glazed tiles with fewer people around.
text.geographic_location: Yonghe Temple is at 12 Yonghegong Street in Dongcheng District, in the north-eastern part of central Beijing. It is a large walled temple complex in the middle of a busy city neighbourhood.
text.directions_text: Ask a taxi driver for Yonghegong Street in Dongcheng District, and head for the temple's main entrance at the southern end. Allow time to queue at busy periods. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the wide view of the courtyard and its buildings into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched look. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for roof tiles, eaves and carved details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at 雍和门 (shoot from below the entrance archway, looking in toward the courtyard). The red walls and golden roof tiles framed by the gate archway, a classic opening shot of the temple. From here the red walls and golden roof tiles sit in front of you along the temple's central line.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and line the buildings up with the edges of the screen so the frame looks straight. Let the red walls fill the sides and the golden roofs sit in the upper part of the picture. For a different view, the Wanfu Pavilion at the north end shows its gilded upper facade and covered walkway, and the Guozijian street nearby has red walls and green glazed tiles with fewer people.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the golden roof tiles to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the bright sky does not wash out the colours. A Live Photo can be useful when people are walking through the scene, because you can pick the frame with the fewest figures in it. Remember that photography is not allowed inside the halls.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early on a weekday morning, when it is quietest. Weekends, Chinese holidays and the 1st and 15th of the lunar month are the busiest times.

text.access_note: This is a working temple and a popular visitor site, so check the official site before you go for entry arrangements, and note that photography is not allowed inside the halls.
claims_not_in_sources: The ultra-wide lens helps fit the wide view of the courtyard and its buildings into one frame.
Tapping on bright roof tiles and lowering the exposure slider helps stop the sky washing out the colours.
A Live Photo lets you choose a frame with fewer people in it when visitors are passing through.
The temple entrance area can have queues at busy times.

name: Jingshan Park
label: Jingshan Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '万春亭' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '万春亭' (way/685673149): middle (25 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/29201967: large area 'Jingshan Park' (699 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Hilltop pavilion with the classic view over the Forbidden City.

text.description:
Jingshan Park is an imperial park of about 23 hectares directly north of the Forbidden City. Its centrepiece is Jingshan, the 'Prospect Hill', an artificial hill about 45.7 metres high. It was raised in the Ming dynasty from soil dug out when the palace moats and nearby canals were made. The hill has five peaks, each with a pavilion, and together they mark the rough line of Beijing's central axis. The park opened to the public in 1928.

It photographs well because the summit pavilion, 万春亭, gives the broadest view over the Forbidden City's rooftops. From the south side of the summit the palace stretches away along the central axis. Turn round and you can pick out the Drum and Bell Towers to the north, with the White Pagoda of Beihai to the west. The classic postcard view is taken facing south. The railing fills up late in the day, so arrive early if you want a place at the front.

If you have time, 观妙亭 looks east to the modern CBD towers. The red walls and yellow-tiled halls of 寿皇殿 suit a tidy, symmetrical shot with fewer people around. On your phone, keep the horizon level, shoot a few frames as people move through, and then take a wider panorama.
text.geographic_location: Jingshan Park is in Xicheng District, in the middle of Beijing. It sits immediately north of the Forbidden City, on the far side of New Jingshan Street and the palace moat.
text.directions_text: Start from the Forbidden City: the park's south entrance is across Jingshan Front Street from it. Beijing Bus routes 101, 103, 109, 124, 202, 211, 609 and 685 serve that entrance. The west entrance is a short walk from the east gate of Beihai Park, and the north entrance is currently closed. Once inside, follow the paths and stone steps up to the summit pavilion, 万春亭. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the classic south-facing view of the Forbidden City. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the railing is crowded and you can only reach a corner, or to take in more of the roofs and sky. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out single halls, or the Drum and Bell Towers when you turn to face north.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (south-facing center point of the summit). The full Forbidden City laid out south along the central axis, with the Drum and Bell Towers to the north and the White Pagoda of Beihai to the west. The viewpoint to climb to is the summit pavilion, 万春亭, which is a separate spot on the hill.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line the central axis up with the middle vertical line, keeping the horizon level. Include a little foreground railing or pavilion roof to give the view depth. For variety, use 0.5x or panorama mode for the wide sweep, then telephoto for tighter details. If you want an alternative, 观妙亭 looks east to the modern CBD towers, which contrast with the old rooftops behind you.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky or the roofs to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour. For a panorama, hold the phone upright and sweep slowly. A Live Photo can capture people moving along the railing.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Arrive well before sunset to get a spot at the railing, and aim for the hour before sunset for warm light. Crowds are heavy at sunset and at weekends.

text.access_note: Jingshan Park has an entrance charge and the summit is reached by stone steps, so it is not step-free; check the official site for opening hours and gate rules before you go.

name: Chairman Mao Memorial Hall
label: Mao Mausoleum
camera_source: Commons cluster (3 photos), weak. Moved 54 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 140 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/8848142: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Chairman Mao Memorial Hall' (163 m across).

text.description:
The Chairman Mao Memorial Hall is the final resting place of Mao Zedong, who led the People's Republic of China until his death in 1976. It stands in the middle of Tiananmen Square, on the site of the Gate of China, which was the southern main gate of the Imperial City in the Ming and Qing dynasties. The hall is a broad, low, columned building, about 160 m across, and it sits squarely in the open square, so you can photograph it with nothing in front of it except the paving and passing visitors.

Construction began soon after Mao's death in September 1976 and was finished on 24 May 1977. Materials came from across China, including granite from Sichuan and pine trees from Yan'an. It closed for nine months of renovation in 1997 and reopened on 6 January 1998.

That distance lets you fit the full width of the building in one frame and keep some of the square around it, which shows how large the space is. Keep your phone level and use the gridlines so the long roofline stays straight. Please be respectful when photographing: this is a memorial where visitors pay their respects. Access to the square and the hall can change, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In the middle of Tiananmen Square in central Beijing, on the site of the former Gate of China, the southern gate of the Imperial City.
text.directions_text: Check the official site before you go for current entry arrangements. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole building. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the columns and roofline. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of open square around the hall.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Tiananmen Square (open ground in front of the mausoleum's main entrance, facing south). The mausoleum set in the middle of the wide square, with the Tiananmen gate and Mao portrait behind you to the north.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the base of the building on a lower line so the roofline sits level. Leave some paving in the foreground to show the scale of the square. Wait for a gap in the crowd, or let a few people walk through the frame for scale. Zoom in to 2x or 3x for a tighter picture of the columns if the full view feels too distant.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to set focus, then lower the exposure slider slightly if the sky is bright, so the sky keeps its colour and the walls don't wash out. Take a few frames, since people keep moving through the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or later in the afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people than the middle of the day. Check the official site for the day's access arrangements before you plan your visit.

text.access_note: This is a memorial inside a busy, controlled public square, so entry and photography rules can change; check the official site before you go.

name: National Museum of China
label: National Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '中国国家博物馆' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/8607825: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'National Museum of China' (396 m across).

text.description:
The National Museum of China stands on the eastern side of Tiananmen Square. It is a huge, calm, stone-fronted building, and that scale is what makes it work in a phone photo. The front has ten square pillars at its centre and runs for 313 metres, so it fills a wide frame even from across the square. It was finished in 1959 as one of the Ten Great Buildings marking ten years of the People's Republic, and it was built to balance the Great Hall of the People opposite. After four years of renovation it reopened in March 2011. Its front has also been used for countdown clocks before big national occasions, including the 2008 Beijing Olympics.

The best photo here is taken from the front steps on the square side. From there you can look across the square towards the Great Hall of the People and the Monument to the People's Heroes. Visitors often sit on these steps towards the end of the day and shoot the buildings opposite, and the warm late light is flattering. The best time of day for the facade can vary, so check the light on the day. Use the steps or a railing to steady your phone, because tripods and drones are not allowed on the square. If you want the museum itself in the frame, walk out into the square and turn round.
text.geographic_location: In central Beijing, on the eastern side of Tiananmen Square, facing the Great Hall of the People across the square.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is given for this spot, so head for Tiananmen Square and look for the long, columned building on its eastern side. The phone icon on the map shows the museum, so use it only as the museum's location. The viewpoint described here is the front steps on the square side, a short walk from the icon. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the Great Hall of the People across the square. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) when you want the whole open square. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the Monument to the People's Heroes.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Go to the front steps of the National Museum of China (中国国家博物馆), on the square side. From the steps, your photo shows the Great Hall of the People and the Monument to the People's Heroes across the square.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the horizon level so the big buildings do not lean. Put the Monument or the Great Hall on one third line and leave the open square in the foreground. For a different view, Tiananmen Square shows the museum's long columned east facade, with people walking past for scale. The Monument to the People's Heroes gives a wide, symmetrical view of the whole square.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the pale stonework to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the facade keeps its detail. For the full width of the building, try panorama mode and move slowly. Brace your elbows on the steps or a railing rather than using a tripod. Inside, flash is banned and some temporary exhibitions do not allow photos, so check signs before you shoot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, close to the 5 PM closing time, when the light turns warm.

text.access_note: The square outside is public, but the museum itself needs advance booking with a passport, so check the official site before you go.

name: Beihai Park
label: Beihai Park
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '五龙亭' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '五龙亭' (node/6896751343): point; moved 20 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/366464114: large area 'Beihai Park' (1419 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.

text.description:
Beihai Park is a former imperial garden just northwest of the Forbidden City, and it has been open to the public since 1925. Its lake covers more than half of the roughly 71 hectares, and at the centre sits Jade Flower Island, topped by the White Dagoba. This Tibetan-style stupa is about 40 metres high and made of white stone. It was built in 1651 to honour a visit by the 5th Dalai Lama. That gives you a bright white landmark against water and trees, which is easy to spot and simple to frame on a phone.

The classic view is from the Five Dragon Pavilions on the lake's north shore. These are five linked pavilions with upswept eaves, built under the Ming. From here the White Dagoba rises across the water. Guides often single this out as the best place in the park for the dagoba, particularly in late light. If you want the pavilions and their reflections in the foreground, with a calm, mirror-like effect, shoot from the opposite lakeshore instead.

For a different angle, the Yong'an Bridge gives a frontal view of the dagoba above the trees with water on both sides. The west shore near the Wanfo Tower is reported to give a view with the dagoba and Jingshan Park's Wanchun Pavilion in one frame; check the exact standing point on the day.

Take a few shots from each spot, keep the dagoba off-centre, and let the water or the pavilion roofs (when shooting from the opposite shore) do the framing.
text.geographic_location: Beihai Park is in central Beijing, immediately northwest of the Forbidden City. Its lake joins Shichahai at the northern end.
text.directions_text: Head for Beihai Park, just northwest of the Forbidden City; no station is listed for this spot, so check a map app for the route. The centre of Beihai Park lies to the south-east, about 9 minutes on foot from there. Inside, follow the lakeshore rather than cutting across, and check the park's opening times on the day. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the water and the dagoba together. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the White Dagoba closer without walking. Try the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you are close to the pavilions and want their roofs to fill the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at 五龙亭 (north shore of the lake; shoot from the opposite lakeshore for the reflection). The White Dagoba on Qionghua Island seen across the water, with the five pavilions and their reflections in the foreground. The centre of Beihai Park is to the south-east of here.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and put the dagoba on one of the upper thirds, with the water along the bottom. Keep the horizon level so the water looks calm. The pavilion roofs and their reflection only appear in the frame when you shoot from the opposite shore. As an alternative, try the Yong'an Bridge for a frontal view of the dagoba above the trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the dagoba to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the white stone keeps its detail against the sky. Take a Live Photo too, in case a ripple spoils the reflection and another frame looks better.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is soft and the dagoba looks best.

text.access_note: Beihai Park is a public park, but entry arrangements and opening hours for some areas can differ, and the inner gardens are reported closed on Mondays, so check the official site before you go.

name: Wangfujing
label: Wangfujing Street
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '王府井天主堂' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '王府井天主堂' (way/85902975): middle (68 m across); moved 10 m off buildings.

text.description:
Wangfujing is a well-known pedestrian shopping street in Beijing, and the church at its northern end is the most photogenic place on it. St. Joseph's Catholic Church (王府井天主堂), also called the East Church, has white Romanesque spires and a brick facade. Behind it rise the modern shopping buildings, which makes a good contrast of old and new. The front plaza and lawn give you a clear, open view of the church, and the exterior is free to photograph. Guides call this the most popular check-in spot on the street. The church is lit up in the early evening, so it looks very good as the light fades.

The street's name comes from a well of sweet water found among the Qing-dynasty princes' residences: "Wangfu" means prince's residence and "Jing" means well. Until the late 1990s the street was open to traffic. Changes in 1999 and 2000 made most of it pedestrian only, so you can now walk its length easily. It has around 280 shops, and the snack street just to the west sells kebabs and candied fruit on sticks.

For the best photo, stand on the plaza facing the church and keep the spires straight against the gridlines. Wait for the lights to come on at blue hour. If you want the busy side of Wangfujing, walk back south onto the main street. There the neon signs and crowds make a lively second shot.
text.geographic_location: Wangfujing is in Dongcheng District in central Beijing. The church stands at the northern end of the pedestrian shopping street, next to the Beijing apm mall.
text.directions_text: Take Beijing Subway Line 1 or Line 8 to Wangfujing station, at the crossing of Wangfujing Street and Chang'an Avenue. The street starts at the Wangfujing South Entrance, by Oriental Plaza and the Beijing Hotel. Walk north along the pedestrian street until it ends at the church and the Beijing apm. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole church and its plaza. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close to the front and cannot fit the spires in. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the brick and the spires.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (front plaza and lawn, facing the church). The church's white Romanesque spires and brick facade, framed against the surrounding commercial buildings, with the illuminated church at blue hour. The main Wangfujing street runs away to the south behind you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the spires up with the vertical lines so they stay upright. Keep a little lawn in the foreground to give depth. For a second shot, walk south onto Wangfujing Street (王府井大街) and photograph the neon signs and the crowd moving towards you. Another option is the front of the Wangfujing Department Store, with the Zhang Binggui statue in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the church to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the lit facade does not blow out. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone steady against a railing or your body. On the busy street, a Live Photo can catch the movement of the crowd.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Around sunset into blue hour, when the church lights come on. One guide gives about 5:30 PM, but this changes with the season.

text.access_note: The street and the church's front plaza are open to the public and the exterior is free to photograph, but the church interior has fixed visiting times, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Sunset and the time the lights come on change through the year, so 5:30 PM is only a rough guide.
The ultra-wide lens helps if you are standing close to the church front.
The street is likely to be crowded in the evening.
Policies on photography inside shops and malls vary from place to place.

name: Shichahai
label: Houhai Lakes
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '银锭桥' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '银锭桥' (way/816148132): middle (13 m across); moved 5 m off water.
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-17: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Lakeside area with bars and old hutongs.

text.description: Shichahai is a historic area of three linked lakes, Qianhai, Xihai and Houhai, in the north of central Beijing. It covers about 147 hectares and dates back to the Jin Dynasty. Under the Yuan Dynasty it was the northern end of the Grand Canal, so it grew into a busy trading district. The name means roughly "the lake of ten temples", and the shores still have temples, old mansions and tall trees. For photos, the best-known spot is 银锭桥 (Yinding Bridge). Guides call it the classic Shichahai view, and it is one of the Eight Views of Yanjing, "Yinding Viewing the Mountains". From the bridge you look west along the water towards the Western Hills, with moored boats in the foreground and sunset light on the lake. It is a simple scene that works well on a phone: water, boats, a layer of rooftops and a soft skyline. Expect a crowd at sunset, so arrive early and be patient for a clear gap at the railing. One guide says the west side gives cleaner compositions. If you want a different angle, the terrace at 糖房咖啡 looks over the hutong roofs and Houhai, with the Drum Tower and Bell Tower in the same frame. It is a café with a minimum spend, so it is not free to use. Venue names vary, so check the signage.
text.geographic_location: Shichahai is in the north of central Beijing, northwest of the Forbidden City and near the north gate of Beihai Park.
text.directions_text: No station is given for this spot, and no public transport details are available. Shichahai is northwest of the Forbidden City and near the north gate of Beihai Park. Look for 银锭桥 (Yinding Bridge) at Shichahai. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the bridge, lake and boats. Switch to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pull the Western Hills and distant rooftops closer. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) when the bridge is busy and you want the whole lake and sky.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on 银锭桥 (west side of the bridge). Looking west from the bridge toward the Western Hills, with the lake, moored boats and sunset light on the water. The wider Shichahai area lies just to the north.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and set the water line on a lower third, with the sky above. Use the railing or a moored boat as a foreground edge. Keep your phone level so the lake looks flat. For an alternative, the terrace at 糖房咖啡 gives a high view over the hutong rooftops with the Drum Tower and Bell Tower in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Sunset light behind the scene can make the foreground dark. Tap the bright sky to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little to keep the colours. Tap a boat instead if you want more detail in the foreground. After dusk, try night mode and rest your elbows on the railing to keep it steady. Live Photos can catch ripples and passing boats.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon into sunset. One guide says after 3 PM for the west-facing backlight, another suggests around 5 PM. In winter, golden hour falls around 4:30 to 5 PM. The bridge gets crowded at sunset.

text.access_note: The lakeside and bridge are public places, but check the official site before you go for any closures or restrictions; the café terrace has a minimum spend.

name: Nanluoguxiang
label: Nanluoguxiang
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Drum Tower' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Drum tower' (node/11934496069): point.
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-17: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).

text.description: Nanluoguxiang is a narrow lane in the middle of old Beijing that gives its name to a whole neighbourhood of hutong, the traditional alleys and courtyard houses. The lane is about 800 metres long and runs from Gulou East Street in the north to Di'anmen East Street in the south. It was built in the Yuan Dynasty and took its current name in the Qing Dynasty, around 1750. Today it is lined with cafés, bars, live music venues and souvenir shops, and a few old courtyard houses linked to famous historic and literary figures. That mix is why it photographs well: grey brick, tiled roofs and shopfronts give you plenty of texture and colour. The flip side is that the main lane is very busy, so a clean, empty view of it is hard to get. For a calmer picture, you can go to the north end near the Drum Tower and shoot the red walls at the side of the tower rather than the crowded front. They frame the top of the hutong area with its grey roofline and put far fewer people in your shot. If you have time, the side lanes are worth a look too. Dong Mianhua Hutong has an arched brick gateway, grey walls and red gates. Beiluoguxiang is a quieter neighbouring hutong with a more local feel. Keep your phone ready for small details such as doorways, lanterns and rooftops, which often make better pictures than the wide crowd scene.
text.geographic_location: Nanluoguxiang is in Dongcheng district, in the old centre of Beijing. The lane runs between Gulou East Street and Di'anmen East Street, with the Drum Tower at its northern end.
text.directions_text: Take the Beijing Subway to Nanluogu Xiang station, which is near the south entrance of the lane. From there, walk north along the lane towards Gulou East Street and the Drum Tower. The lane is about 800 metres long, so allow extra time if you stop to look in the shops. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the lane and the red walls. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the side walls are too close to fit in. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the grey roofline or a detail such as a gate or lantern without stepping into the crowd.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Drum Tower (north end of Nanluoguxiang; use the red walls on the side rather than the crowded front of the tower). Red walls and the tower's grey roofline, framing the north end of the hutong area with fewer people in the frame than at the front.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line a red wall up with one of the vertical lines, with the grey roof across the top third. Keep your phone level so the walls do not lean. For a different view, walk into Dong Mianhua Hutong and shoot along the side lane at the arched brick gateway, which keeps the lane's crowd out of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the red wall to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the red stays rich and the sky does not wash out. Portrait mode works well for a person standing in front of the wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Check on the day when the lane is quietest. Soft daylight suits the red walls and grey brick.

text.access_note: The lane and the side streets are open public streets. The red walls at the side of the Drum Tower are outside the tower and can be photographed from the street.

name: Drum Tower of Beijing
label: Drum Tower
pin_note: Position from OSM W267371087 (Drum Tower): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.

text.description:
The Drum Tower of Beijing is a landmark building that is easy to spot and rewarding to photograph. Its solid, traditional shape gives you a strong subject, and the phone icon on the map is a short, easy distance away, so you can fit the whole building into one frame without fuss. From there the tower sits straight ahead to the north, about 70 metres away, which makes it simple to line up a clean, symmetrical shot.

The tower is big enough to stand out against the sky, and its roofline is the part that catches the eye. Start with a wide view that shows the full building and a little of the street around it. This gives a sense of place that a close crop cannot. Then step in or zoom to pick out details such as the roof edges and other architectural details.

Take a few frames at different zoom levels, because the view changes quickly as you move. Check the edges of the screen for passers-by, signs and cables, and wait a moment if someone walks through your picture. Keep your phone upright for the height of the tower, then turn it sideways for a broader scene. Opening and access conditions are not covered here, so check locally before you go.
text.geographic_location: The Drum Tower is in central Beijing.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so use a map app to reach the Drum Tower area. Walk straight north towards the building and look for the best angle as it grows larger. The phone icon on the map is about 70 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the full tower from where you stand. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for roof and architectural details. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you move much closer and cannot fit the whole building in.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 70 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. From here the full building should sit in the middle of the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the tower on the centre line so the sides look balanced. Keep your phone level so the walls do not lean. Leave a little space above the roof for sky. Then take a second shot with the telephoto lens to fill the frame with the upper part of the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the colours of the building stay rich. Try a Live Photo to catch people passing by, and pick the best frame afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon is usually kinder to the colours than midday sun. If the light is flat, wait for a brighter moment.

text.access_note: Opening and access conditions are not covered here, so check locally before you go.

name: Zhengyangmen
label: Qianmen Gate
camera_source: Commons cluster (33 photos). Moved 12 m outwards on 2026-11-10 so it is 200 m from the subject's edge, as the text says.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/25109960: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Zhengyangmen' (113 m across).
notes: The Front Gate tower south of Tiananmen Square.

text.description: Zhengyangmen, better known as Qianmen, is a Ming-era gate in Beijing's old city wall. It stands just south of Tiananmen Square and once guarded the southern entrance to the Inner City. It was first built in 1419 and the gate complex was heavily rebuilt in 1914. At 42 metres, the gatehouse is the tallest of all the gates in the city wall, and it is one of the few that still has its main tower. That height is why it photographs so well. Its tiered roofs and tall grey walls stand out clearly above the low buildings and street furniture around it. The city's central north–south axis passes through its main gate, so a straight-on view from the south gives you a naturally balanced, symmetrical picture. The separate archery tower stands south of the gatehouse, across Qianmen Avenue, so it may be in the foreground when you face north from the phone icon on the map, and it is another good subject. The phone icon on the map is about 200 m south of the subject. That is far enough to fit the whole tower in the frame without tilting your phone upwards. Keep the phone level and use the gridlines so the vertical walls stay straight. Wait a moment for people to walk out of the foreground, or include a few as a sense of scale. For a closer, tighter picture, walk towards the gate rather than relying on digital zoom.
text.geographic_location: Zhengyangmen (Qianmen) is in central Beijing, just south of Tiananmen Square. It sits at the northern end of Qianmen Street, on the city's central north–south axis.
text.directions_text: Beijing Subway Lines 2 and 8 serve Qianmen. You could also start from Tiananmen Square and head south to the gate, or take a taxi to the Qianmen area. From there, face north and the gatehouse is straight ahead. The phone icon on the map is about 200 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole gate and some of the street. Switch to telephoto (2x or 3x, depending on your phone) for a tighter, more compressed view of the tower. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you walk much closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 200 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. The gate should sit centrally in your frame, with the tall tower in the middle.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the main gateway on the centre line so the picture is symmetrical. Keep the phone upright and level so the walls do not lean. Leave a little sky above the roof. Try one wider shot with the street in the foreground and one telephoto shot of the tower alone.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the gate to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the roofs keep their detail. Hold the phone steady with both hands and take two or three frames.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows on the tower. Early in the day is also likely to be quieter.

text.access_note: The gate can be photographed from the surrounding streets, but the gatehouse is a tourist attraction, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.

label: Bell Tower

text.description:
The Bell Tower of Beijing is a tower that makes a strong, simple subject for a phone photo. The shape is easy to read from a distance. The tower's outline and the strong vertical lines stand out against the sky, and you can try to fit the whole building into the frame without special equipment.

The phone icon on the map is about 130 m south of the subject. From there you can look north and take in the tower as a whole. It is about 2 minutes on foot from the phone icon on the map, so you can take a few frames from different spots without losing much time.

Take a first photo with the default lens (1x) to show the tower in its setting, then move to 2x or 3x for a tighter, cleaner shot of the upper part of the tower. Turn on the gridlines and line the tower up with a vertical line so the walls stay straight. Tap the tower on screen to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the tower keeps its colour and detail. Hold the phone with both hands and take a couple of frames in case people walk through the view. Check current visiting information locally before you go.
text.geographic_location: The Bell Tower stands in central Beijing.
text.directions_text: No Underground station or tram stop is listed for this spot; use a map app to reach the Bell Tower area in central Beijing. From the phone icon on the map, walk north towards the tower. The phone icon on the map is about 130 m south of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the whole tower. Switch to telephoto (2x-3x) for the upper part of the tower. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you move much closer.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 130 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line one edge of the tower up with a vertical grid line so it does not lean. Leave a little sky above the top of the tower. At 2x or 3x, fill the frame with the upper part of the tower. Take one wide shot and one close shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little if the sky is bright. Do not use portrait mode, as it is meant for people and close objects, not a distant building.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually gives the best colour on the tower.

name: National Centre for the Performing Arts (China)
label: National Grand Theatre
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'National Centre for the Performing Arts' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/4974233: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'National Centre for the Performing Arts' (270 m across).
notes: The glass-and-titanium dome known as 'The Egg'.

text.description: The National Centre for the Performing Arts is a huge dome of titanium and glass sitting in its own lake, immediately west of Tiananmen Square and the Great Hall of the People. Locals call it "the Boiled Egg", and from the water's edge you can see why. It was designed by the French architect Paul Andreu and opened in 2007. The shell is about 212 metres long and 46 metres high, and it is made of more than 18,000 titanium plates with a band of glass running up the middle. The lake wraps all the way around it, and visitors reach the halls through a long passage under the water, so nothing breaks the smooth outline. That is what makes it easy to photograph: one clean shape, a lot of reflection, and plenty of space around it. The east lakeshore, across the water from the building, is a good place to stand. It shows the whole dome as a backdrop, which works well for full-length portraits or silhouettes against the lit shell, and it is usually quieter than the main entrance. Aim for blue hour, when the sky still has colour and the building lights are on. If you want a second angle, try the street trees along Xi Chang'an Jie. Frame them in the foreground with the dome rising behind, so the soft leaves contrast with the metal. Keep your phone steady against your body or a railing, and wipe the lens first.
text.geographic_location: In Xicheng district, central Beijing, on the south side of Chang'an Street, immediately west of Tiananmen Square and the Great Hall of the People.
text.directions_text: Head for Tiananmen Square and the Great Hall of the People; the dome stands immediately to the west, on the south side of Chang'an Street. The building's address is No. 2 West Chang'an Avenue. Once there, walk around the lake to the east shore, which is on foot and not by a named bridge. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the dome and its reflection. If you cannot fit the whole shell in from the lakeshore, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x). Use the telephoto (2x-5x) only for tighter shots of the titanium surface or people on the far side.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The recommended viewpoint is the east lakeshore, across the water from the building, a short walk away around the lake. From there the full dome fills the background, which suits full-length or silhouette shots against the lit shell.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the dome centred, with the waterline on a lower grid line so the reflection has room. For a silhouette, put your subject against the lit shell and keep the whole figure inside the frame. For an alternative view, try street trees on Xi Chang'an Jie in the foreground with the dome rising behind.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the dome or your subject to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the lit shell keeps its colour and silhouettes stay dark. As the light fades, use night mode, but rest your elbows on a railing and hold still for the full capture.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Blue hour, roughly 6:30–7:30 pm, when the shell is lit and the sky still has some colour.

text.access_note: The lakeshore and the building's outside are open-air, but going inside is ticketed and photography during performances is not allowed, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The whole length of the building may need the ultra-wide (0.5x) lens from close to the lake edge.
Lowering the exposure slider helps keep the lit shell's colour and gives cleaner silhouettes.
The time of blue hour shifts through the year, so the 6:30–7:30 pm window is only a rough guide.
Night mode works best when the phone is held still against a railing or your body.

name: Monument to the People's Heroes
label: People's Heroes Monum.
camera_source: Researched viewpoint '天安门广场' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap '天安门广场' (relation/941596): edge nearest the subject (827 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/8847722: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Monument to the People's Heroes' (90 m across).
notes: Obelisk at the centre of Tiananmen Square.

text.description:
The Monument to the People's Heroes is a ten-storey granite obelisk in the southern part of Tiananmen Square, standing just in front of the Mausoleum of Mao Zedong. It honours those who died in the revolutionary struggles of the 19th and 20th centuries. At 37.94 metres tall, it rises alone from the open square, so it makes a clean, simple subject for a phone photo. Architect Liang Sicheng led the design, and building ran from August 1952 to May 1958. The front carries Mao Zedong's handwritten inscription, 'Eternal glory to the people's heroes', and the base is inlaid with eight large and two small relief panels showing major events in modern Chinese history. It has been a nationally protected heritage site since 1961.

The wide, open space around it is the main advantage. From the middle of the square you get a clear view with nothing in the way, and the Tiananmen Gate and the big state buildings frame the obelisk. The monument also works well as a foreground subject for photos of the gate. For a different picture, a close, low-angle shot shows the granite and the marble reliefs around the base. Barriers keep you back from the monument itself, so work from where you are allowed to stand. Expect security checks and large crowds, and go early or late in the day for softer light.
text.geographic_location: In the southern part of Tiananmen Square, in central Beijing, just in front of the Mausoleum of Mao Zedong.
text.directions_text: Head for Tiananmen Square in central Beijing and walk into the open square. Expect a security check on the way into the square. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the obelisk with the gate and buildings around it. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want the whole open square, and to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the inscription and relief panels from behind the barriers.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in 天安门广场 (centre of the square, shooting from the north or south approach). The obelisk standing alone in the open square, with the Tiananmen Gate and surrounding state buildings framing it. For a close, low-angle view of the granite and the reliefs at the base, stand as near as the barriers allow.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn the phone upright to show the full height of the obelisk, with a little empty sky above the top. Switch on gridlines and keep the sides of the monument parallel to the vertical lines. To make the monument a foreground subject, place it to one side and let the Tiananmen Gate show behind it. A close, low-angle shot of the base is a good alternative.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stone to set focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the sky does not turn white. Do not shoot straight into the sun, as faces and the shadowed side of the stone will go dark.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer. Avoid noon, when strong backlight darkens faces.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space with security checks and large crowds, and barriers keep visitors away from the monument's base; tripods and drones are not permitted, so check the official site before you go.
